options: A join that requires no ON clause
A join between two completely unrelated tables
A special keyword, SELF JOIN, distinct from other join types
A table joined to itself, using two different aliases
questions.explain: There's no special syntax — it's the same JOIN you already know, just applied to one table listed twice.

questions.q: Why does a self join always need two different aliases for the same table?
options: Without them, SQL Server has no way to distinguish one row's role from the other's, since both come from the same table
Aliases are required syntax for any JOIN, self or otherwise
It's purely stylistic and has no functional purpose
Because ON clauses cannot reference unaliased tables
questions.explain: In the manager example, 'e' and 'm' both come from Employee, but represent different roles — the employee vs. their manager.

questions.q: In the real AdventureWorks2012 example, what does the pAssembly alias represent?
options: The finished/assembled product
A part used inside another product
The product's category
A customer who purchased the product
questions.explain: pAssembly refers to Production.Product joined via BillOfMaterials.ProductAssemblyID — the finished product.

questions.q: In that same example, what does pComponent represent?
options: A duplicate of the BillOfMaterials table
A component/part that goes into the assembled product
The employee who manufactured the product
The same row as pAssembly, just relabeled
questions.explain: pComponent is joined via BillOfMaterials.ComponentID — a different role for the same underlying Product table.

questions.q: Is a special SELF JOIN keyword required in T-SQL?
options: No — any JOIN type (INNER, LEFT, etc.) can be used as a self join simply by referencing the same table twice
Self joins require a stored procedure
Yes, SELF JOIN is a distinct keyword separate from INNER/LEFT/RIGHT
Self joins can only use FULL OUTER JOIN
questions.explain: The BillOfMaterials example uses ordinary INNER JOIN twice — 'self join' describes a pattern of usage, not new syntax.
